opus-5.5.text:
I think healthcare is one of the clearest cases where more wealth and better technology translate directly into things people care about. If you ask what you'd actually want to buy if you were much richer, past a certain point it's not a bigger house or a nicer car. It's more years of healthy life. People already spend enormous amounts on healthcare, especially near the end of life, and that tells you how much they value it, even though what they're buying right now often isn't very effective.

So what excites me is the prospect that AI and the broader growth it could drive would make that spending actually work. Today a lot of medical progress is bottlenecked by how slow and expensive research is: the long timelines for drug discovery, clinical trials, and our limited understanding of biology, especially aging. If you had very capable AI systems doing a lot of that research, plus a much larger economy to fund it, you could plausibly see much faster progress against things like cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, and maybe aging itself.

And aging is the big one for me. Most of the disease burden in rich countries is downstream of getting old. If you could meaningfully slow or reverse that, it would be worth more than almost any consumer product I can think of. You're not buying a slightly better version of something you already have; you're buying more time and more health to enjoy everything else. That's why, when I think about what a much richer future would offer, healthcare stands out as the area where the gains could be most dramatic and most widely valued.

r001.rationale: The response says people spend heavily on healthcare and value more healthy years, but does not state that they may pay a great deal to eliminate non-life-shortening conditions that cause daily inconvenience.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that makes healthcare stand out is that it's the category where I personally have the most unmet demand, and where the gap between what I'd pay and what's currently available is largest. For most goods, if you look at the consumption basket of someone like me, I'm already pretty close to satiated. I can buy the food I want, the housing I want, more entertainment than I could ever consume. The marginal dollar doesn't buy me much more utility. But with health, that's just not true. There are things I would pay enormous sums for that nobody can sell me at any price right now.

The obvious one is longevity. If someone could sell me an extra twenty or thirty healthy years, the amount I'd be willing to pay for that is some substantial fraction of my lifetime income. And I don't think that's unusual. When you survey people or look at revealed preferences, the value of a statistical life that governments use is on the order of ten million dollars, and that's for an average person over their remaining lifespan. So the willingness to pay is clearly there. It's not a demand problem. It's purely a supply problem, and the supply problem is a technological one.

And then beyond lifespan there's just the enormous space of things that currently degrade quality of life that we accept as inevitable. Declining cognitive performance as you age, loss of mobility, chronic conditions that aren't fatal but make every day a bit worse. If you could buy a treatment that kept your cognition at age-thirty levels into your eighties, that's a product that basically everyone in the world would want, and right now it doesn't exist.

So the reason I find it exciting in the context of AI progress specifically is that if you believe AI is going to substantially accelerate the rate of scientific and technological progress, healthcare is where that shows up most directly as something I personally get to buy. A lot of other economic growth is somewhat abstract from the perspective of an individual consumer. If GDP doubles, maybe my house is nicer, maybe I take more vacations, but the change in my day to day experience is kind of modest. Whereas if biomedical progress accelerates by the same factor, the products that come out of that are ones that change my life in a way I actually notice and care about a lot.

There's also a sort of interesting economic point here, which is that this is one of the clearest cases where current GDP measures would undercount the gains. If you cured aging, the measured GDP contribution would be whatever people pay for the treatment, but the actual welfare gain would be vastly larger than that. So I think when people try to estimate how much AI could improve living standards by extrapolating from historical growth rates in measured output, they're probably missing a lot of what matters, and healthcare is where most of what they're missing lives.

r001.rationale: The response mentions nonfatal chronic conditions that make daily life worse and says people would want treatments for age-related decline. But its explicit willingness-to-pay claim concerns extra years of life, not eliminating these non-life-shortening conditions.

astra-6.text: I think healthcare is exciting because it’s an area where, even if you have a lot of money today, there are things you simply can’t buy. If you have a disease that we don’t know how to treat, being wealthy might get you better care, but it doesn’t necessarily solve the problem. So the exciting prospect is that we develop treatments that actually expand what’s possible—curing diseases, preventing them, or letting you stay healthy for longer. That seems much more valuable to me than getting a slightly nicer version of something I can already buy. You’re getting more time, and more ability to enjoy that time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curing diseases and extending healthy life, but does not state that people may pay a great deal to eliminate non-life-shortening conditions that cause daily inconvenience.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s exciting to me is the possibility of buying more healthy time. A lot of things you can spend money on make your life a little more comfortable, but better healthcare could let you do things you otherwise couldn’t do at all. If you can prevent a disease, restore some lost ability, or slow down aging, that potentially changes your whole life.

And there’s a lot of room for improvement. Today, even if you have a tremendous amount of money, there are many health problems you simply can’t pay to have solved. So future medical progress could expand what’s available to buy in a way that another improvement in an ordinary consumer product doesn’t.

r001.rationale: The response says future healthcare could solve health problems and restore abilities, but it does not specify willingness to pay a great deal for conditions that cause daily inconvenience without shortening life.
